ch5_ex1_q1: Difference-of-squares shortcut: $c^2 - b^2 = (c-b)(c+b)$, so $w^2 = (7.3-2.41)(7.3+2.41) = 4.89 \times 9.71 = 47.4819$. Fewer big squares to key in.
Sanity check: the base is short, so $w$ should be only a little less than the hypotenuse 7.3. An answer of about 6.9 fits.
ch5_ex1_q2: Spot the pattern: sides $x$ and $2x$ always give a hypotenuse of $x\sqrt{1+4} = x\sqrt{5}$. So $x\sqrt{5} = 5$ gives $x = \sqrt{5}$ straight away.
ch5_ex1_q3: The vertical triangle is 12, 16, 20, which is the 3, 4, 5 triple multiplied by 4, so the half-diagonal is 12 with no calculator.
A square's side is its diagonal divided by $\sqrt{2}$: side $= 24 \div \sqrt{2} = 12\sqrt{2} \approx 16.97$ cm.
ch5_ex1_q4: Difference of squares makes this quick: $32^2 - 30^2 = (32-30)(32+30) = 2 \times 62 = 124$, so the overhang is $\sqrt{124} \approx 11.14$ cm.
Draw the cross-section as a rectangle with a right-angled triangle on each side. This trapezium picture works for any truncated cone (frustum).
ch5_ex1_q5: Estimate to check: $\sin 20^\circ \approx 0.342$ and $\sin 21^\circ \approx 0.358$, so $\sin(20^\circ 37')$ must lie between them. 0.3521 does.
Remember $37' = \frac{37}{60}^\circ \approx 0.62^\circ$, so the angle is about $20.62^\circ$, not $20.37^\circ$.
ch5_ex1_q6: Benchmark: $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$ and cosine decreases as the angle grows. Since 0.5712 is a bit more than 0.5, $\theta$ must be a bit less than $60^\circ$.
Calculator technique: press $\cos^{-1}(0.5712)$ then the DMS (degrees-minutes-seconds) key to see $55^\circ 10'$ directly, instead of converting 0.166 of a degree by hand.
ch5_ex1_q7: Mnemonic: SOH-CAH-TOA ("Some Old Horses Can Always Hear Their Owners Approaching"). Opposite and adjacent are both known here, so it is TOA.
Spot the triple: 2.4 and 3.2 are $0.8 \times 3$ and $0.8 \times 4$, so $\tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}$. The 3-4-5 triangle's angles are always about $36.87^\circ$ and $53.13^\circ$.
ch5_ex1_q8: In any isosceles triangle, the line from the apex down to the base is perpendicular to it and cuts the base in half. That turns the problem into right-angled triangles with adjacent side 5.9.
Quick check: $y$ is a hypotenuse, so it must be longer than 5.9. An answer of 6.7 fits.
ch5_ex1_q9: Since $62^\circ > 45^\circ$, $\tan 62^\circ > 1$. So the height above eye level must be more than the 12 m distance, which is a quick way to check your working.
Option D (207.56) is close to what you get by adding 185 instead of 1.85 m, which shows why converting units first matters.
ch5_ex1_q10a: Quick rules for $\theta$ from compass form: N$\theta$E $= \theta$, S$\theta$E $= 180-\theta$, S$\theta$W $= 180+\theta$, N$\theta$W $= 360-\theta$. For N$20^\circ$E the bearing is just 020$^\circ$T.
ch5_ex1_q10b: S$\theta$W means $180 + \theta$: $180 + 47 = 227^\circ$T. Check that it lands between 180 and 270, which is the south-west quadrant.
ch5_ex1_q10c: N$\theta$W means $360 - \theta$: $360 - 33 = 327^\circ$T. Think of it as turning 33° back anticlockwise from north.
ch5_ex1_q10d: S$\theta$E means $180 - \theta$: $180 - 17 = 163^\circ$T. Check that it lands between 090 and 180, which is the south-east quadrant.
ch5_ex1_q11: Eliminate fast: both angles share the same height, but the edge angle has a longer horizontal distance (half-diagonal), so it must be smaller than $55^\circ$. That rules out B and C.
The two horizontal distances differ by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ ($3.6$ versus $3.6\sqrt{2}$), so $\tan(\text{edge angle}) = \tan 55^\circ \div \sqrt{2}$.
ch5_ex1_q12: Compass-form shortcut: swap both letters. $032^\circ$T is N$32^\circ$E, so the reverse is S$32^\circ$W $= 180 + 32 = 212^\circ$T.
Check: a bearing and its back bearing always point in opposite directions, so they must be in opposite quadrants (NE and SW here).
ch5_ex1_q13: Convert $220^\circ$T to compass form: $220 - 180 = 40$, so it is S$40^\circ$W. Both legs then head west, so their west components add.
Pattern: if the angle is measured from the north-south line, sin gives the east/west part and cos gives the north/south part.
ch5_ex1_q14: Formula to remember for two angles of elevation along a line: $h = \dfrac{d}{\frac{1}{\tan A} - \frac{1}{\tan B}}$, where $d$ is the distance between the observers.
Check the order: the bigger angle ($41^\circ 16'$) belongs to the closer point Q, because you look up more steeply when you are nearer the mountain.
ch5_ex1_q15: A $45^\circ$ angle in a right-angled triangle makes it isosceles, so the vertical side equals 8 with no trig needed.
Then $\tan(25^\circ 13') = \frac{8}{8+x}$, so $8 + x = \frac{8}{\tan(25^\circ 13')} \approx 16.99$. The smaller angle gives a longer base, as expected.
